# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Overview

This repo is **hasToggle.dev** — the unofficial live playground for Next.js and Vercel. The product is `apps/web`: a lab of chapters that each open on a belief a developer holds and run the real feature next to it. See `README.md` for the shape of the lab and where the chapter code lives.

The monorepo around it was scaffolded from [next-forge](https://github.com/vercel/next-forge) (`npx next-forge init` — a one-time copy, no upstream, no shared history). It uses Bun workspaces and Turborepo. The other apps and most of `packages/*` came with the scaffold and are not part of the site.

## Development Commands

### Setup & Installation
```bash
bun install                    # Install all dependencies
```

Set `MONGODB_URI` in the environment (validated via @t3-oss/env-nextjs in `packages/database/keys.ts`).

### Running Applications
```bash
bun dev                       # Run all apps in development mode
turbo dev --filter=app         # Run only the main app (port 3000)
turbo dev --filter=web         # Run only the web/marketing site (port 3001)
turbo dev --filter=api         # Run only the API (port 3002, includes Stripe webhook listener)
```

### Testing
```bash
bun test                      # Run tests across all workspaces
turbo test --filter=app        # Run tests for specific app
bun test                       # Run Bun test runner in apps/app or apps/api
```

### Code Quality
```bash
bun run check                     # Run Biome linter/formatter checks (uses ultracite presets)
bun run fix                       # Auto-fix linting/formatting issues
turbo boundaries               # Check package boundaries
```

### Building
```bash
bun run build                     # Build all apps (depends on tests passing)
turbo build --filter=app       # Build specific app
turbo analyze --filter=app     # Analyze bundle size
```

### Database

The database is MongoDB, accessed through the official `mongodb` driver — there is no ORM, no schema migrations, and no generated client. `packages/database/index.ts` exports a `database` object with typed collection handles; document types live in `packages/database/types.ts`.

### Maintenance
```bash
bun run bump-deps                 # Update dependencies (excludes recharts)
bun run bump-ui                   # Update shadcn/ui components
bun run clean                     # Clean node_modules from root
turbo clean                    # Clean build artifacts and node_modules from all workspaces
```

## Architecture

### Monorepo Structure

The repository uses **Bun workspaces** with two main directories:

- **apps/** - Deployable applications (independently deployable)
- **packages/** - Shared packages consumed by apps

### Applications (apps/)

1. **app** (port 3000) - Main SaaS application
   - Authentication via better-auth (route groups: `(authenticated)` and `(unauthenticated)`); handler mounted at `/api/auth/[...all]`
   - Uses Next.js 16 with App Router
   - Server actions in `app/actions/`
   - API routes in `app/api/`
   - Tests configured with Bun test runner

2. **web** (port 3001) - Marketing/landing page
   - Internationalization support (uses `[locale]` route)
   - Content management via CMS package
   - Rate limiting via Arcjet

3. **api** (port 3002) - RESTful API server
   - Health check endpoint at `/health`
   - Webhook handlers in `app/webhooks/`
   - Cron jobs in `app/cron/`
   - Development includes Stripe webhook listener (requires Stripe CLI)

4. **email** - Email templates (React Email)
5. **storybook** (`apps/storybook`) - Component development environment.
   Its package name is `@repo/storybook`, **not** `storybook`: Bun links every
   workspace package into the root `node_modules` by name, so a workspace named
   `storybook` shadows the real `storybook` npm package and every addon that
   imports `storybook/internal/*` fails to resolve. Turbo filter is
   `--filter=@repo/storybook`. Never name a workspace after one of its own
   dependencies.
6. **studio** - Database management UI (stale Prisma Studio wrapper; non-functional since the MongoDB migration)

### Shared Packages (packages/)

Core infrastructure packages:

- **@repo/auth** - better-auth authentication (client, server, middleware, provider)
  - MongoDB adapter + organization plugin; the active org id is the tenant id
  - Server instance in `instance.ts`; `server.ts` is a Clerk-shaped compat layer
    (`auth()`, `currentUser()`) so callers did not have to change
  - Handler mounted by apps/app at `/api/auth/[...all]`
- **@repo/database** - MongoDB via the official `mongodb` driver (server-only)
  - Typed collection handles exported from `packages/database/index.ts`
  - Document types at `packages/database/types.ts`
  - Requires `MONGODB_URI` (validated in `packages/database/keys.ts`)
- **@repo/design-system** - shadcn/ui component library
  - Components in `components/` (auto-generated, excluded from Biome linting)
  - Providers for themes, tooltips, etc.
  - Dark mode support via next-themes
- **@repo/observability** - Sentry error tracking and logging
- **@repo/security** - Arcjet integration for application security
- **@repo/analytics** - Google Analytics and PostHog
- **@repo/payments** - Stripe integration
- **@repo/email** - Resend email service
- **@repo/webhooks** - Webhook handling (inbound/outbound)

**The dashboard needs BOTH repos mirrored.** Sessions hang off checkpoints, which join to *code* commits by the `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer. Mirroring only the checkpoint sidecar makes entire.io render it as an ordinary repo — raw commits and files, zero sessions. Fixed 2026-08-27: installed the Entire GitHub App on `hasToggle/hasToggle.dev` + `entire repo mirror create github.com/hasToggle/hasToggle.dev aws-eu-central-1.entire.io` → 50 sessions indexed immediately.

**Both mirrors are in `eu` (aws-eu-central-1); the account's home jurisdiction is `us`.** Consequence: `entire activity`/`recap` default to the US cell and read empty — use `entire api --jurisdiction eu`. **Cloud `entire dispatch` is broken by this** (404 "not available in its region"; the endpoint doesn't exist on the EU cell either). Use `entire dispatch --local`, which generates through the installed Claude Code CLI. Keep the mirrors in eu anyway — LfD Niedersachsen.

**Redaction (PR #407, 2026-08-27):** `redaction.pii.enabled` + `externalize_images` on. `externalize_images` is bloat control, NOT privacy — the `assets/` subtree is pushed unredacted, and images are exempt from all nine redaction layers by design. `pii.address` matches US addresses only. `goredact` needs CLI >0.10.2. Happened once (checkpoint 1072cb2379b0); rewritten with a force-push of `entire/checkpoints/v1` on the checkpoints repo and the local `.entire/metadata/<session>/full.jsonl` redacted the same way so a later finalize does not re-push it. See [[feedback-no-pii-in-tool-output]].

description: Never print subscriber emails, partial emails, or their domains in tool output; transcripts are public via entire.io

**PIVOT (2026-07-31):** Eric reconsidered the 2026-04 AI-misconceptions direction. hasToggle.dev is now **the live playground for Next.js & Vercel** — interactive demos of real features running on the page itself, aiming to eventually cover "everything Next.js has to offer" plus as much of the Vercel platform as can be demoed from a page. Audience: bootcamp grads → seniors (Eric's bootcamp-coach background is the trust anchor). The old landing (5 misconception demos, three-moves/Values, misconceptions route) was deleted; the masterclass and learn pages survive unlinked.

**Funnel (locked):** weekly digest form (kept — email capture is load-bearing) promising "one new exhibit every Monday", and **paid small cohorts** where Eric coaches; cohort seats announced to the list first. Playground itself stays free, permanently.

**Built-in-public angle:** repo is public; the site is built with AI (Conductor driving Claude Code) and the process is published via Entire.io as part of the curriculum. "The site is its own biggest demo." (Checkpoints repo is public since 2026-08-20 and linked from the landing page and lab chapter making-of strips.)

**Three-layer model (2026-08-21, Eric's articulation — direction, mostly settled):**
1. **The lab** (`/lab`, built) — live running references, mechanism-truth,
   audience-agnostic, a destination. The demos are their own abstraction
   layer.
2. **Learning paths** (`/learn` territory) — narrative, goal-directed
   routes through the lab's landmarks, shaped per audience (beginner /
   junior / senior crossing over) and per *constraint* (e.g. the feature
   inside a multi-tenant app — "the feature within a constrained
   environment"). Open question whether cohort-gated or public; **Eric
   leans public**, not formally settled.
3. **The cohort** — paid structured experience that *relies on* existing
   demos and paths, adds recorded video or live streams; where
   comprehensive ground-up web development gets taught, depending on the
   cohort run.
The boundary rule that fell out of discussion: the lab doesn't know who's
reading; a path knows exactly who's reading. design.md's four-audience /
no-per-level-modes rule is the lab's half of that contract. Existing
/learn content is proto-specimens of the other layers (ref-vs-state,
qa-stories, parked Hazel counter = path lessons; the masterclass = a
cohort-layer artifact whose beat transport could become the path
sequencing primitive).

**What carried over from the old positioning:** the three-layer voice (Surface plain / Meta Pratchett-dry `MetaAside` asides / Demo reveals), the editorial design system (Switzer + JetBrains Mono, plus-grid, ht-cyan, § dividers, numbered-chapter Contents), and the "real, not simulated" demo ethic. The Wittgenstein/ownership thesis and "three moves" copy are retired from the page; don't resurrect them in new copy.

**Technical positioning choice (2026-07-31):** apps/web runs `cacheComponents: true` — the landing page teaches the current Next 16 model (use cache / cacheLife / cacheTag / updateTag / PPR / Suspense streaming) by running it on itself. First five exhibits: boundary (server vs client), shell (re-bake this page), stream, mutation (cookie counter), image (/api/og). Roadmap section lists ~10 upcoming exhibits; "new exhibit every Monday" is the content cadence Eric committed to on-page.

**How to apply:** new landing copy and demos serve the playground thesis (show, don't tell; real behavior with honest readouts; link official docs from every exhibit). Cohort/digest copy stays no-asterisk honest about what's paid.

When the conversation grows long, some or all of the current context is summarized; the summary, along with any remaining unsummarized context, is provided in the next context window so work can continue — you don't need to wrap up early or hand off mid-task.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

Reach for this when the task matches an available agent type, when you have independent work to run in parallel, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate it and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps. description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

# Privacy and Redaction Configuration Overview

This documentation covers how to configure privacy settings in Entire, a system that manages checkpoint metadata and sensitive data protection.

## Key Configuration Areas

**Secret Scanning**: By default, Entire uses Betterleaks to detect API keys, tokens, connection strings, and private keys. You can enable goredact as an alternative or run both scanners simultaneously. Both are configurable in `.entire/settings.json`.

**PII Redaction**: Disabled by default, this optional layer redacts email addresses, phone numbers, and street addresses when enabled. The system allows custom pattern definitions that produce labeled redaction tokens like `[REDACTED_EMPLOYEE_ID]`.

**Custom Redaction Rules**: Users can define project-specific patterns using Go RE2 syntax. These can be stored as inline rules in settings files or as reusable YAML/JSON rule packs in the `.entire/redactors/` directory.

**OpenAI Privacy Filter (OPF)**: An optional ML-based layer that catches names and personal data regex patterns might miss. It requires the `opf` binary installation and configuration of at least one detection category. The system offers environment variable overrides for single pushes.

**Image Handling**: The `externalize_images` setting moves base64-encoded images from transcript files into an `assets/` store, reducing file size but not affecting redaction scanning.

**Telemetry**: Users can opt out of anonymous usage analytics via settings or the `ENTIRE_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT` environment variable.

**Commit Signing**: Checkpoint commits are signed by default using existing Git signing keys, configurable per repository or machine.

All settings live in either committed `.entire/settings.json` (team-wide) or local `.entire/settings.local.json` (personal only).

content.content:
# Security & Privacy Summary: Entire

## Data Location

Entire stores AI session checkpoints in **your own Git repository**, not on external servers. Specifically:

- **Refs-based storage** (default): `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>`
- **Branch-based storage** (older): `entire/checkpoints/v1`
- **Shadow branches**: Temporary working storage during sessions, containing unredacted source snapshots—Entire doesn't push these
- **Local configuration**: `.entire/` directory (mostly gitignored)

As the documentation states: *"Checkpoints live in **your** Git repository, not in a service Entire controls."*

## Redaction Layers Before Write

Nine sequential redaction layers process content:

| Layer | Type | Applies To |
|-------|------|-----------|
| 1-5 | Pattern/entropy matching | Every write (entropy, secret patterns, provider tokens, URIs, connection strings) |
| 6 | User-defined rules | When configured |
| 7 | Credential value detection | Every write |
| 8 | PII detection | When enabled |
| 9 | OpenAI Privacy Filter | Push time only; branch backend only |

**Critical limitation**: *"Treat redaction as a safety net rather than a guarantee."* Source-file snapshots on shadow branches receive no redaction.

## Data Transmission

Entire transmits data in these scenarios:

| Trigger | Destination | Content | Redacted? |
|---------|-------------|---------|-----------|
| `git push` | Your Git remote | Checkpoints + code | Yes |
| `entire checkpoint explain --generate` | Summary provider | Compacted transcript | Yes |
| Telemetry | PostHog | Command/flag names, hashed machine ID | N/A (no transcript) |

## Residual Risk & User Responsibility

**Public repositories** pose inherent risk: anyone with read access sees all checkpoint content. The documentation emphasizes: *"If your repository is public, so are they."* Users should maintain private repositories for sensitive work and review checkpoints before pushing.

content.text:
## The short version

Keep the transcripts public — but stop letting them be *automatic*. The leak you're worried about isn't hypothetical (2026-09-14, 124 partial addresses + ~30 company domains, fixed by force-push), and it came from exactly the class Entire structurally cannot catch. The fix is to split sessions by data class, not to go dark.

---

## What entire.io actually offers for publishing sessions

There is **no session-level publishing primitive**. No share links, no embeds, no per-session visibility, no "publish this one." What exists is two independent surfaces:

**1. Your Git repo — the one that's actually world-readable.** Checkpoints are ordinary commits in a repo *you* own. Entire's own docs are blunt: *"Checkpoints live in your Git repository, not in a service Entire controls… If your repository is public, so are they."* `hasToggle.dev-checkpoints` being public on GitHub is your decision, not a platform feature. Nothing about it is revocable — force-push leaves unreachable objects fetchable by SHA, and forks/archives/caches persist.

**2. entire.io mirror visibility — a different, much weaker "public."** `entire repo visibility set <repo> public|private`. "Public" here = read-only pull for **any authenticated Entire user**; push and management stay with grantees. Both your repos currently read `visibility: public` on `aws-eu-central-1`. They're `foreign: true` / `canManage: false`, so this tracks GitHub collaborator permissions rather than being independently settable. `entire grant repo add/remove` gives named-user access when private.

**Withholding granularity: all-or-nothing.** `entire configure --skip-push-sessions` (and it accepts `--local`, so it can live in `.entire/settings.local.json` — your machine only, not the team file). There is no per-session opt-out flag.

**Redaction knobs you're not using yet.** Current settings run `pii.email` + `pii.phone` + `externalize_images`. Available and unused:
- **Custom RE2 rule packs** (`.entire/redactors/*.yaml`, or inline) producing labeled tokens — this is what would catch `REDACTED` and a domain denylist.
- **`pii.address`** — US patterns only, so worthless for German addresses.
- **OPF (OpenAI Privacy Filter)**, layer 9 — the ML pass that catches *names and prose* the regex layers miss. Push-time only, **branch backend only**. You're on the branch backend, so it's available — but it's the thing that pins you there while `refs` is now the recommended backend.

Entire's own framing of all nine layers: *"Treat redaction as a safety net rather than a guarantee."*

---

## Assessment of the offering

The lab is the product. The transcripts are **evidence**, not product — and they're load-bearing evidence: they're what makes "this site is its own biggest demo" a claim instead of a slogan, and they're the single most credible artifact behind a paid cohort where you coach people on driving agents. Dropping them costs you a real differentiator.

But notice the actual value distribution. Nobody reads 480 raw JSONL transcripts. Almost all the credibility comes from *the link existing and being checkable*; the teaching value comes from the curated making-of strips on chapter pages. The risk, meanwhile, is the opposite shape: unbounded, permanent, and concentrated in a minority of sessions.

Three things make the current model wrong-shaped rather than merely risky:

1. **The site now has live subscriber data.** Every session touching Mongo, Resend contacts, or the reconcile endpoint is a session over 104 real people's addresses. That wasn't true when you made the repo public on 2026-08-20.
2. **Regex redaction is blind to prose.** The leak wasn't a raw dump — it was partial addresses and domains in tool output and my own summaries. No scanner layer models "the assistant is narrating third-party data." OPF narrows this; it doesn't close it.
3. **It isn't yours to consent to.** You can publish your own prompts. You cannot consent on behalf of subscribers. A subscriber-data disclosure in a public repo is an Art. 33 notifiable breach to LfD Niedersachsen inside 72h — and partial address + employer domain is still personal data where re-identification is reasonably possible.

---

## Options

| | Approach | Cost | What it leaves on the table |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | Harden redaction in place: custom rule pack (starred partials, domain denylist), enable OPF | ~half a day | Narrows the funnel; prose leaks and novel shapes still pass. Blast radius stays "everything, forever." |
| **B** | **Split by data class** + A as safety net | ~a day, plus a habit | Nothing meaningful. |
| **C** | Capture private, hand-publish selected sessions | High, ongoing, no tooling | Quietly falsifies "wrong turns included." |
| **D** | Go private | Free | A genuine differentiator, for a risk B already handles. |

**Recommendation: B, with A underneath it.**

Concretely: production-data work stops happening in the tracked repo. Sessions that touch Mongo, Resend contacts, or Vercel env run in a separate private ops repo (or with `--skip-push-sessions` in `.entire/settings.local.json`). What remains in the public checkpoints repo is exactly what the positioning claims to publish — the lab's code, copy, and design sessions, wrong turns included. The hardening layer stays on as backstop, not as the primary control.

**Trade-offs to name:** enabling OPF keeps you on the branch backend, so you defer the `refs` migration. The split adds a decision point at the start of any data-touching session — that's friction, and friction is where this fails; it needs to be a settings-file fact, not a thing you remember. And "every prompt and checkpoint published as they happen" (`page.tsx:139`) becomes slightly overstated — it'd want to become "every prompt behind the lab," which is honest and costs nothing.

**Two things worth doing regardless of which option you pick:** the 2026-09-14 force-push didn't reach forks, clones, or GitHub's cached views — a one-time audit of the already-published archive for subscriber data, and a GitHub support request to purge cached views if anything's still reachable. And the `assets/` subtree is pushed **unredacted by design** — `externalize_images` is bloat control, not privacy, so any screenshot of the Resend dashboard or a Mongo result set is sitting there in the clear and no layer ever looked at it.

Want me to draft the redactor rule pack and the ops-repo split, or audit the published archive first?

content.thinking:
I'm checking whether sensitive transcripts can be selectively dropped before pushing, rather than needing a separate repo. So far I've confirmed there's no per-session opt-out flag, `--skip-push-sessions` is all-or-nothing but can be set locally, and the checkpoint backend is currently branch-based.

The real ambiguity is whether "drop" means preventing publication in the first place versus scrubbing something already pushed—the latter being the force-push approach that doesn't truly unpublish. Feasibility of the former depends on push mechanics: even if a session is held back locally, its data still lives in `.entire/metadata/<session>/full.jsonl`, and I recall a past instance where redacting that file manually was necessary to stop a later finalize from re-pushing it—meaning held-back sessions can silently leak unless manually cleaned up each time.

I want to verify this rather than assume, so I should check `entire clean`, session stop, and session deletion commands, plus the actual behavior of `--skip-push-sessions` once re-enabled. There's also a cleaner alternative worth considering: doing sensitive, data-touching work in an untracked scratch directory outside any git-tracked repo entirely, so Entire never captures it in the first place—avoiding the whole retroactive-scrubbing problem.

content.content:
# Session Management in entire.io

Based on the provided documentation, there is **no information addressing** your questions about:

- Deleting, hiding, or excluding individual sessions from push

content.text:
Neither, quite. Dropping works but it's the wrong *kind* of control — and "separate repo" was heavier than it needs to be.

## Why dropping is weak

There's no supported per-session opt-out. To hold one session back you'd do roughly: `entire configure --skip-push-sessions --local` **before** starting → do the work → `entire clean --session <id>` → clear the staged transcript → re-enable. Four manual, order-dependent steps, and `entire clean` doesn't even cover the whole surface — its help lists session state, shadow branches, and `.entire/tmp/`, but **not** `.entire/metadata/`, which is where the transcript stages. That's exactly why the September 14 cleanup needed the local `full.jsonl` edited by hand: otherwise a later finalize re-pushes the same content you just force-pushed away.

And dropping *after* the fact isn't dropping. The force-push rewrote the branch, but unreachable objects stay fetchable by SHA on a public repo until GitHub GCs (which it doesn't do promptly), and forks, clones, and archives are untouched. You get to clean three places, retroactively, under pressure.

The structural problem: this control has to fire *before* the session, on a session you haven't recognised as sensitive yet — and its failure mode is silent. The September 14 leak wasn't a lapse in discipline, it was a probe that didn't look dangerous until it printed.

## What I'd actually do

**1. The rule pack — do this regardless.** The leak had a *shape*: `REDACTED` and bare domains. A `.entire/redactors/*.yaml` pack catches that shape on every session forever, needs no discipline, and costs one file. This is the single highest-value change and it would have prevented the actual incident.

**2. Then decide where ops work lives** — and notice that the sensitive sessions aren't code sessions. The contact classification, the Mongo restore, the Resend reconciliation: none of it changed a line of `apps/web`. It's operational work that happens to run in this worktree out of convenience.

Two structural options, and the deciding factor isn't privacy:

| | Cost | Privacy | Your own history |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Scratch dir**, Entire not enabled | `mkdir` | ✅ never captured | ❌ lost — no `entire search` over it |
| **Private repo**, Entire enabled | ~15 min setup | ✅ captured, unpublished | ✅ kept and searchable |

Both solve the leak identically. The private repo wins on the thing you'd actually miss — you lean on `entire search` and the memory system for recall, and ops work is exactly the kind you want to look up six weeks later ("how did I classify those contacts last time?"). A scratch dir throws that away to save fifteen minutes.

So: **private repo, for the history, not for the privacy.**

**3. Keep dropping — as incident response.** It's the right tool when something slips past 1 and 2. It's the wrong tool as the primary gate.

The awkward case worth naming: sessions that do both, like the resignup hardening — it changed `apps/web` *and* ran the contact restore. Those split across two windows. Slightly annoying, and honestly better hygiene than what's happening now.

Want me to write the redactor pack first? It's the part that pays off immediately and doesn't depend on the repo decision.

# hasToggle-ops

Private. Operational work against live hasToggle.dev data — MongoDB subscribers,
Resend contacts, segment and broadcast state.

## Why this repo exists

`hasToggle/hasToggle.dev` publishes every agent session to a **public** checkpoint
repo, and the site says so on the landing page. That is deliberate and worth
keeping. It is also incompatible with running scripts over 100+ real subscriber
addresses: on 2026-09-14 a contact-classification run put 124 partial addresses
and ~30 employer domains into a public transcript, which took a history rewrite
to pull back — and a force-push does not un-publish anything already fetched,
forked, or cached.

Entire has no per-session opt-out. The only reliable control is *where the
session runs*. So:

| Work | Repo |
|---|---|
| Site code, copy, demos, design | `hasToggle.dev` (public sessions) |
| Anything reading or writing subscriber records | **here** (private sessions) |

Sessions are still captured here — checkpoints live in this repo, so
`entire search` and `entire why` keep working across ops history. They are
simply never published.

A session that needs both (harden the signup route *and* repair the contact
list) splits in two. That is mildly annoying and better hygiene than the
alternative.

## Rules for agents working here

Read `CLAUDE.md`. The short version: even in a private repo, subscriber detail
never goes to stdout — counts and buckets only, identifying rows to a gitignored
file under `.context/`. Private today is not private after the first time this
repo gets a collaborator.

## Setup

```bash
bun install          # if/when there are deps
cp .env.example .env # MONGODB_URI, RESEND_TOKEN
```

`.env` is gitignored and stays that way.

# CLAUDE.md

Operational scripts against live hasToggle.dev data. See `README.md` for why
this repo is separate from `hasToggle/hasToggle.dev`.

## The one rule that matters

**Subscriber detail never reaches tool output.** Not full addresses, not
two-letter prefixes, not starred partials (`REDACTED`), not bare employer
domains, not counts broken down finely enough to identify one person — and not
in prose summaries either, which is where it actually leaked last time.

What stdout may contain: totals, and coarse buckets (`freemail` vs `other`).

What identifying rows are for: a file under `.context/`, which is gitignored.
The human opens it themselves.

This holds **even though this repo is private**. Private is a setting, not a
property; it survives exactly as long as nobody adds a collaborator or flips
the toggle. The habit is the protection.

## Redaction

`.entire/redactors/hastoggle-pii.yaml` is the same pack as the public repo —
masked-email shapes, waitlist confirm tokens, Resend keys, webhook secrets.
It is a safety net under the rule above, not a replacement for it. Entire's own
docs: *"Treat redaction as a safety net rather than a guarantee."* Regexes
cannot see an agent narrating third-party data in a sentence.

## Data sources

- **MongoDB** — the `subscribers` collection behind the waitlist. Same Atlas
  cluster as production. Treat every write as production, because it is.
- **Resend** — contacts, segments, broadcasts. Full-access key required for
  contact operations; a sending-only key fails silently on them.

Both live in `.env`. Never echo an env value, and never pass one as a visible
CLI argument.

## Writing scripts

Default shape for anything that reads people:

```ts
// read → classify → write detail to .context/, print only the tally
const rows = await collection.find(...).toArray();
await Bun.write(".context/audit.json", JSON.stringify(rows, null, 2));
console.log(`${rows.length} records · ${freemail} freemail · ${other} other`);
```

Destructive operations (delete, bulk update) are two-phase: a dry run that
reports counts, then an explicit `--apply`. No exceptions — the contact cull on
2026-09-14 went through 140 records and got that right; keep it.

## 1. Redactor pack — `.entire/redactors/hastoggle-pii.yaml` (commit `21c19e81`)

|---|---|---|
| `masked-email` | `REDACTED`, `h•••@`, `ha…@`, `ha..@` | `pii.email` needs a real local part — this is the exact shape that leaked |
| `subscriber-token` | `\b[a-f0-9]{64}\b` | the waitlist confirm token *and* its sha256 lookup hash; a published token is a live capability against one subscriber's record |
| `resend-api-key` | `re_…` | belt and braces over the secret scanners |
| `webhook-signing-secret` | `whsec_…` | same |

**The pack is committed, so it deliberately holds no data.** A denylist of actual subscriber domains would publish exactly what it's meant to hide — those belong in `.entire/redactors/local/`, which is gitignored. I didn't generate one: it would redact every mention of a common domain across all transcripts for modest gain, and the stdout discipline is the better control for that vector.

Verified: all 16 samples pass (checked directly against the patterns — RE2 subset, no lookarounds, so the check is faithful), and `git grep` finds **zero** 64-hex strings in any tracked file, so `subscriber-token` costs nothing in false positives. `entire status` runs clean with the pack in place. - **Claude Code hooks are out of date** — "some or all hooks may silently not fire." Fix: `entire enable --force`. Worth doing promptly; silently-not-firing capture hooks are their own problem.
- **2 stuck sessions**, one from today 16:43 — the session that *handled* the leak, ended with uncondensed checkpoint data on a shadow branch. Shadow branches are unredacted but never pushed, so it isn't exposure; it does want cleaning. `entire doctor` can't prompt in this non-interactive session.
